frontMatter.title: Propaganda and persuasion
frontMatter.description: How did wartime propaganda try to influence Australians on the home front, and what can historical sources tell us about its purpose and impact? Analyse two authentic posters, test the limits of their evidence and build a short historical argument. Write your responses in your exercise book.

frontMatter.title: What you will learn
frontMatter.description: Practise three historical skills using evidence from Australian WWII posters.
intentions: Identify a source’s origin, intended audience, purpose and message in its historical context.
Distinguish observation, supported inference and claims that the evidence cannot establish.
Explain how origin and purpose affect a source’s usefulness for a particular inquiry.
Compare persuasive messages and write a short argument using details from both sources.

introduction.why: Propaganda is designed to persuade. Its words and images can show what its creator wanted people to think or do, rather than what everyone actually believed.
introduction.keyIdea: Read origin, audience, purpose and message together; support interpretations with visible details.
method: Identify who produced the source and when.
Describe a visible detail before explaining its likely meaning.
Distinguish the creator’s intention from the audience’s actual response.

activities.title: The home front and the sources

notes.body: During WWII, civilians were encouraged to support the war effort through work and everyday choices. This lesson examines two government-produced posters, not the whole wartime experience.

The Australian War Memorial identifies Source A as a 1943 Department of Commerce and Agriculture poster. Its collection explanation connects growing food at home with reducing demands on commercial supply and transport.

The Memorial identifies Source B as a 1942 Department of Information poster. It presents a threatening Japanese advance. The hostile caricature is a wartime racial stereotype to analyse critically, not a factual portrait of Japanese people.
The posters are primary sources for wartime persuasive messages. Their present-day Memorial catalogue descriptions are later interpretations and metadata, not words spoken by wartime audiences.

visual.alt: Australian wartime poster showing a smiling woman in overalls with a garden fork. Large lettering asks Australians to do their bit on the Food Front and grow their own Vegetables for Victory. Checked in the authoring interface.

examples.prompt: In your exercise book: identify the creator and date; suggest the intended audience; describe two visible details; then explain the action the poster encourages. Which part of your answer is an observation, and which is an inference?

steps.text: The department is known from the catalogue; the individual artist remains unknown.
Observation: a smiling woman with a garden fork appears beside an instruction to grow vegetables.
Inference: the poster addresses Australians able to grow food at home, including women; the image does not establish that only women were targeted.
Purpose: it connects an everyday activity with national contribution, presenting food growing as a positive way to help the war effort.

activities.title: Guided application: Source A
activities.practiceNote: Respond on paper. Refer to sources by A or B and explain how each detail supports your reasoning.

questions.stem: Explain one persuasive technique in Source A.
parts: Choose and describe one visible detail before interpreting it.
Complete: The poster presents … ; this may encourage its audience to … because … .
Identify one group whose experience is not represented by the image. Explain why a single poster cannot represent everyone.

sourceMetadata.rights: Copyright expired — public domain, as recorded by the Australian War Memorial

examples.prompt: Without opening Model analysis, write 4–5 sentences identifying the origin, likely audience, purpose and message. Use two specific visible details. Explain how the threatening image tries to influence attitudes; do not claim that all Australians reacted in the same way.

steps.text: The catalogue dates Source B to 1942 and identifies the Department of Information as its maker.
The soldier’s large figure, gun and movement towards Australia present an immediate threat.
The slogan links survival to fighting or working; fear and urgency are used to encourage participation.
This is evidence of the department’s persuasive message, not proof of invasion plans or a universal public response.

introduction.why: A source can be useful for one question and limited for another. A persuasive purpose is something to analyse, rather than a reason to discard a source.
introduction.keyIdea: Ask what this source can establish for this inquiry, and what additional evidence is needed.
method: Connect usefulness to origin, purpose and a specific question.
State a limitation and propose evidence that could address it.

notes.body: A detail actually visible in the source: an image, a printed instruction or a design choice. Catalogue details such as date and maker come from metadata; identify that basis separately.
A reasoned interpretation supported by details and context: for example, that a threatening image aims to create fear. Use terms such as suggests or aims to when the evidence calls for them.

A poster alone cannot measure how many people changed their behaviour. A diary might reveal one person’s reaction; broader claims need a range of reception evidence and records of circulation or behaviour.

examples.prompt: Classify each claim as observation, supported inference or not established by the poster alone: (1) a soldier is shown approaching Australia; (2) the maker aims to create urgency; (3) every Australian was frightened. Explain whether this source is useful for studying government persuasion and whether it is sufficient for measuring public response.

steps.text: Observation: the image shows a soldier approaching Australia; this is what the poster depicts, not proof that an invasion was planned.
Supported inference: the gun, scale and survival slogan suggest that the maker aims to create fear and urgency.
Not established: the poster gives no direct evidence of every viewer’s feelings or actions.
Its government origin makes it valuable evidence of an official persuasive strategy; its persuasive purpose and lack of audience testimony limit what it can establish about reception.

activities.title: A later account of the poster

notes.body: The Australian War Memorial’s present-day catalogue reports that Source B was considered alarmist and was not released in Queensland or Melbourne. This adds evidence about limits to distribution; it does not measure how every viewer responded. Source: https://www.awm.gov.au/collection/C374232
The catalogue also distinguishes wartime fears from later knowledge about Japanese strategy. Do not turn the poster’s threatening message into proof that an invasion of Australia was inevitable.

activities.title: Guided application: usefulness
activities.practiceNote: Respond on paper. Refer to sources by A or B and explain how each detail supports your reasoning.

questions.stem: Assess Source A for the inquiry: How was home food-growing promoted?
parts: Give one useful feature and connect it to the inquiry.
Explain how its government origin and persuasive purpose affect your reading.
Give one limitation for the different question: How many people grew more food because of this poster?
Propose an additional source and explain what it could establish; identify a remaining limitation.

activities.title: Independent judgement
activities.practiceNote: Respond on paper. Refer to sources by A or B and explain how each detail supports your reasoning.

questions.stem: Write a 90–120 word judgement about Source B’s usefulness for studying attitudes on the home front.
parts: Explain what it reveals about the maker’s intended message using a visible detail.
Separate this from what it cannot establish about audience response.
Use the later catalogue note carefully: identify its status and what it adds.
Suggest corroborating evidence and explain why one personal account would not establish a universal response.

slides.title: Comparing messages and constructing an argument

introduction.why: Comparison is more than describing two sources separately. Explain a meaningful relationship and use evidence to support a claim.
introduction.keyIdea: Both posters promote contribution, but their persuasive strategies and contexts differ.
method: Identify a similarity and a difference using details from both sources.
Explain how those details support your interpretation.
Write a qualified argument and state a limit on claims about impact.

examples.prompt: Compare Sources A and B. Identify one shared purpose and one difference in technique. Explain the perspectives their makers promote. What audience perspectives would you need to investigate separately? Record evidence from both posters before opening Model analysis.

steps.text: Both government-produced posters link civilian action with the war effort: food growing in A and fighting or working in B.
A’s smiling gardener and vegetables present contribution positively; B’s armed soldier and survival slogan make the appeal urgent and threatening.
These represent official persuasive messages from different departments and dates, not the whole range of civilian perspectives.
Audience reactions, disagreement and practical barriers would need other evidence, including personal accounts considered alongside wider records.

notes.body: Answer the question directly: identify how the posters tried to influence attitudes. Avoid claiming that intention proves success.
Use at least one specific detail from each poster; explain how each detail supports the claim instead of only naming it.
State what the evidence cannot establish about impact and what further evidence would help. Use historical terms such as propaganda, home front, purpose, perspective and corroboration accurately.

activities.title: Guided argument plan
activities.practiceNote: Respond on paper. Refer to sources by A or B and explain how each detail supports your reasoning.

questions.stem: Plan an answer to: How did these sources attempt to shape attitudes towards the war effort?
parts: Write a claim that relates the two strategies.
Choose one visible detail from A and explain its persuasive effect as an intended effect.
Choose one visible detail from B and explain the contrast.
Add a sentence distinguishing intended influence from demonstrated public response.

examples.prompt: How did wartime propaganda try to influence Australians on the home front, and what can these sources tell us about its purpose and impact? Write 150–200 words using Sources A and B. Make a clear claim and compare the two messages, rather than writing two disconnected descriptions. Use at least one specific detail from each poster and explain how it supports your argument. Consider origin, context and purpose; distinguish official perspectives from audience perspectives. State a limitation concerning actual impact and identify additional evidence that would help test it.

steps.text: Check that your claim answers the inquiry and relates the two strategies.
Check that a specific detail from each source supports your reasoning.
Check that you distinguish official messages from audience responses and qualify claims about impact.

notes.body: Have you cited specific details from both posters and distinguished observation from inference?
Have you explained a meaningful similarity and difference, and avoided claiming that every Australian reacted alike?
You can explain how the posters sought to persuade. Establishing their actual impact requires evidence beyond the posters. Reaching the final page does not certify mastery.
